HIP removed porosity and raised Σ3 twins in PBF-LB_SS316L from 2.4 % to 33 %.

  * •

## Abstract

This study investigates the effects of Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) on the rotating bending fatigue (RBF) performance of Powder Bed Fused-Laser Beam (PBF-LB) 316L stainless steel (SS316L) at both room (25 °C) and elevated temperatures (450 °C). HIP was applied at 1150 °C and 100 MPa for 4 h following stress relief to eliminate porosity and homogenize the microstructure. Advanced microstructural characterization revealed that HIP reduced porosity below detection limits and transformed the melt-pool structure into an equiaxed grain morphology with a significant increase in Σ3 twin boundary fraction (∼2.4 % to 33 %). These changes were accompanied by reduced dislocation density and internal strain. Fatigue testing showed that HIP specimens exhibited superior high-temperature fatigue endurance (170 MPa) compared to as-built samples (130 MPa), due to defect elimination and microstructural stabilization. However, at 25 °C, as-built specimens outperformed HIP ones (240 MPa vs. 220 MPa) owing to retained work-hardened microstructures. Fractographic analysis confirmed these trends: multiple crack initiation sites dominated as-built failures, while HIP fractures showed single-origin cracks with striation growth. Post-fatigue electron backscatter diffraction maps revealed temperature-dependent grain coarsening and dislocation accumulation, particularly in the as-built samples. Overall, HIP significantly enhanced the high-temperature fatigue resistance of PBF-LB_SS316L by improving microstructural integrity and delaying crack initiation, highlighting the importance of post-processing in AM components.

## 2. Experimental procedure

### 2.1. Materials and methods

In this study, SS316L powder with an average particle size of 37 ± 5 μm and a nominal chemical composition of Cr:16.5–18.5, Mo:2.0–2.5, Mn: ≤2.0, Ni: 10–13, Si: ≤1.0, C: 0–0.03 wt%, and Fe as the base was utilized. Fatigue test samples were designed with two distinct geometries to accommodate testing at both elevated (Fig. 1a) and ambient (Fig. 1b) temperatures.

The samples were fabricated using the PBF-LB process on a GE M2 machine, with process parameters including a laser power of 370 W, a scanning speed of 1350 mm/s, a hatch spacing of 90 μm, a layer thickness of 50 μm, and a laser spot size of 130 μm under constant purge of nitrogen gas (No contouring strategy was applied during fabrication, as the focus of this study was to investigate the bulk fatigue behavior and microstructural response of PBF-LB SS316L in as-built and HIP conditions, without the influence of additional surface-related processing variables) Fig. 1c shows the schematic of the PBF-LB method used to produce fatigue samples. Fig. 1, Fig. 1 illustrate the build plate, including ambient and elevated temperature samples, respectively. Following fabrication, all specimens underwent a stress relief heat treatment at 550 °C for 6 h (Fig. 2a) before being separated from the build plate. After stress-relieving both build plates, the specimens were extracted (Fig. 2b), and a subset from each series was selected for the HIP process.

The HIP process was conducted at 100 MPa and 1150 °C for 4 h, following the ASTM F3184:2024 standard (Fig. 2c). After HIP, the samples were rapidly cooled using argon gas to minimize thermal effects. Subsequently, the specimens were polished and prepared for the RBF (Fig. 2d).

### 2.2. Microstructure characterization

To accurately assess the mechanical and fatigue properties of the samples produced in this study, various microstructural characteristics were evaluated before and after the HIP process, as well as before and after the mechanical testing at both ambient and elevated temperatures. The microstructural analysis was conducted using an optical microscope following sample preparation, according to the ASTM E3:2023 standard [34]. Etching was performed using a solution composed of hydrochloric acid (25 ml), distilled water (25 ml), and copper sulfate (5 g), as specified by the ASTM E407:2023 standard [35]. Imaging was carried out using a Keyence VHX-7000 digital microscope.

For a more in-depth microstructural analysis, an FEI Scios 2 HiVac dual beam system equipped with multiple detectors, including an Oxford Symmetry S3 CMOS electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector, was utilized to investigate the impact of the HIP process and cyclic loading during fatigue testing. The acquired data were subsequently processed using AZtecHKL software, enabling detailed EBSD analyses.

To determine the density of the as-built and heat-treated samples, the Archimedes method was used according to ASTM Standard B311-13 [36]. Moreover, the amount of porosity, pore size distribution, and exact pore morphology were analyzed using the micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) technique. A ZEISS Xradia 520 Versa micro-CT scanner was utilized, operating at 140 kV with an exposure time of 1.0 s per image, a voxel size of 5 μm, and a total of 1601 projections. The acquired data was processed and analyzed using Dragonfly 3.1 software.

### 2.3. Uniaxial tensile and rotating beam fatigue tests

The mechanical properties and fatigue behavior of the samples were assessed both before and after the HIP process. Uniaxial tensile testing was conducted using an INSTRON-5985 tensile machine at a quasi-static strain rate of 1 × 10^{−3} s^{−1}, following the ASTM E8:2022 standard [37], with three repetitions per sample. Uniaxial tensile stress–strain curves before and after the HIP process for PBF-LB_SS316L were extracted.

Fatigue testing was performed using the RBF method at both ambient temperature and at 450 °C, utilizing a Zwick Amsler RBM120T system equipped with an in-situ furnace for high-temperature testing. It is noted that RBF introduces a stress gradient across the gauge section, with the maximum stress localized at the specimen surface. As such, the obtained fatigue limits are not directly equivalent to those from axial fatigue tests. The rotating-bending method was selected due to facility availability and because it accentuates surface-driven fatigue mechanisms, which are particularly relevant in PBF-LB 316L stainless steel. The applied stress during fatigue tests ranged from 86 % to 40 % of the yield strength, and corresponding RBF test results were generated for all samples following ISO 1143 guidelines [38]. The RBF was performed on an in-situ furnace, maintaining the specimen at 450 °C, following ASTM E606:2021 [39]. It should be noted that the reference σ_{y} used for normalization at 450 °C is not an experimentally measured value at this temperature, but rather an estimated strength obtained by extrapolating published 600 °C tensile data within a physically based softening framework. Because we did not perform high-temperature uniaxial tensile tests, this external curve (embedded in a physically based softening framework) served only to set a conservative, mechanistically justified scale for σ_{y}(T). In each test series, a small number of preliminary tests were conducted; thereafter, the stress amplitude was reduced stepwise based on observed results until the runout criterion was reached. This protocol was applied identically to as-built and HIP specimens at both temperatures.

The fracture surfaces of the tested samples were thoroughly analyzed using an SEM at various magnifications to investigate crack initiation and propagation leading to failure. Microstructural modifications at the fracture edges were assessed using the EBSD method. It is important to note that all calculations and measurements in this study were conducted with an uncertainty assessment at a 95 % confidence level, employing a coverage factor K = 2, with each measurement repeated a minimum of three times.

## 3. Results and discussion

### 3.1. Microstructural investigations

#### 3.1.1. Powder characterization

Fig. 3 illustrates the detailed characterization of gas-atomized SS316L powders. The SEM images (Fig. 3a) confirmed that the powders exhibit spherical morphology and smooth surfaces, typical of the atomization process, with a narrow size distribution (D10: 23.8 µm, D50: 38.08 µm, D90: 49.61 µm). EBSD analyses provided further insights into the crystallographic characteristics, where the inverse pole figure (IPF) map (Fig. 3b) shows randomly oriented grains, while the phase map (Fig. 3c) revealed a fully face-centered cubic (FCC) austenitic structure with no detectable secondary phases in the as-atomized condition. Complementary EDS results (Fig. 3e) confirmed the nominal SS316L composition, dominated by Fe, Cr, and Ni with minor alloying elements such as Mo, Mn, and Si.

#### 3.4.1. S-N curve

Fig. 7 reveals significant differences in fatigue performance among the four conditions, in both the endurance limit (horizontal asymptote of the S-N curve) and the slope of the fatigue life curve in the finite-life regime. At ambient temperature, the as-built material showed superior HCF strength compared to its HIP samples, as shown by the blue symbols in Fig. 7. The as-built specimens represent the reference S-N curve from the authors' previous study [66]. In contrast, the HIP samples tested at 25 °C (red symbols) endured a slightly lower stress of around 220 MPa for the same fatigue life (at a runout cycle of 5×106). In other words, under room-temperature conditions, the as-built state maintains a higher fatigue limit than the HIP post-processed state, despite the latter’s elimination of internal porosity. This behavior appears to contradict the conventional understanding of HIP treatment, which typically enhances fatigue performance by reducing internal porosities that act as crack initiation sites. However, this discrepancy can be attributed to the fundamental difference between RBF and uniaxial fatigue tests. In RBF testing, the surface layer experiences the highest tensile stress and plays a dominant role in crack initiation, making it a surface-sensitive fatigue method. Since HIP primarily affects subsurface and internal defects but has limited influence on surface imperfections, the process may not significantly improve surface integrity. The individual data points used to construct Fig. 7, including the applied stress levels and corresponding number of cycles to failure for each condition, are listed in Table 1. Consequently, the as-built specimens, which were polished and retained their original surface characteristics, exhibited superior fatigue strength compared to the HIP samples.

Fig. 7. RBF S-N curves for PBF-LB SS316L in as-built and HIP conditions, tested at room temperature (25 °C, blue and red symbols) and 450 °C (black and green symbols). Thus, in Fig. 7, the polished as-built condition (blue) shows a higher endurance limit than the HIP condition (red), although the HIP data displays scatter (more consistent lives), reflecting the homogenized microstructure and absence of large defects.

At 450 °C, the S-N curves of the as-built and HIP samples showed an opposite behavior compared to their trends at room temperature. As-built specimens tested at 450 °C (black symbols in Fig. 7) suffer a drastic reduction in fatigue strength, with an endurance limit on the order of 130 MPa, roughly half of that observed at room temperature. Moreover, the S-N curve for the as-built/450 °C condition dropped off steeply, indicating extreme sensitivity of fatigue life to stress amplitude at a high temperature. Only a modest increase in stress above the 130 MPa level led to a sharp transition into the finite-life regime (e.g., failures occur well before 106 cycles), suggesting that the as-built material has very limited fatigue resistance once thermal effects come into play. By contrast, the HIP samples at 450 °C (green symbols) demonstrated a much higher endurance strength of about 170 MPa, and their S-N curve was considerably flatter in the HCF regime. Even at 450 °C, the HIP material retained a well-defined fatigue limit (runouts at 170 MPa) and sustained significantly longer lives at a given stress amplitude compared to the as-built material. In summary, whereas elevated temperature caused a dramatic 45 % drop in the endurance limit of the as-built alloy (240 to 130 MPa) alongside a steep S-N slope, the HIP alloy experienced only a relatively modest 15 % reduction in endurance limit (220 to 170 MPa) and preserved a gentle S-N slope with a discernible fatigue threshold.

This study's fatigue data were obtained in RBF per ISO 1143, which creates a fully reversed stress state that peaks at the surface and decreases toward the neutral axis [38]. Because only a small surface volume experiences the maximum alternating stress each cycle, RBF is not directly equivalent to uniform-stress axial fatigue as defined in ASTM E466 [68]. The green S-N curve retains a broad plateau out to 5×106 cycles and only gradually declines at higher stress amplitudes, indicating that fatigue failure in the HIP/450 °C condition is controlled more by the inherent strength of the thermally softened austenitic matrix and the effective microstructural barriers (twin-enhanced grain boundaries) rather than by catastrophic defect-driven crack initiation. In practical terms, the HIP process has preserved a large fraction of the material’s ambient fatigue capability even at 450 °C, whereas the as-built material’s capability has nearly collapsed in that regime. The evolution of fatigue mechanisms with temperature (from primarily defect-governed crack initiation at ambient, to creep-assisted and microstructure-governed failure at 450 °C) is tempered by the HIP-induced improvements in microstructural integrity. This understanding underscores that a combined strategy of pore elimination (via HIP) and microstructural optimization is crucial for ensuring reliable fatigue performance of PBF-LB SS316L, especially for service at elevated temperatures.

Here, the measured strengths decreased to ∼160–180 MPa, reflecting the strong influence of thermally activated mechanisms, such as cyclic softening, oxidation, and enhanced dislocation mobility. While HIP mitigates internal defect sensitivity, the dominant fatigue crack nucleation mechanism under these conditions remains surface controlled, and temperature degradation reduces both as-built and HIP strengths to similar levels. Thus, the empirical correlation between UTS and endurance limit provides a useful link between monotonic tensile response and cyclic performance. Still, temperature-dependent mechanisms must be incorporated to capture the observed degradation in high-temperature fatigue resistance [71,77]. The following Section 3.4.2 further correlates these mechanical fatigue results with the detailed microstructural features observed in as-built vs. HIP samples, providing a deeper insight into the role of grain boundaries, dislocations, and other defects in the governing fatigue behavior.

The combination of low dislocation density, a recrystallized equiaxed grain structure, and abundant twin boundaries effectively suppressed creep-assisted fatigue damage, even at 450 °C. Furthermore, comparing the HIP 450 °C data (green curve) to the baseline 25 °C data (blue and red curves) highlights the remarkable preservation of fatigue strength after HIP, even under severe thermal exposure. Unlike the as-built condition, where high temperatures drastically reduced fatigue life, the HIP material retained a significant proportion of its ambient fatigue life. A reference is provided in the fatigue behavior of PBF-LB_SS316L.

At the elevated temperature (450 °C), additional fatigue damage mechanisms (such as dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding) become operative [18,80]. The as-built sample, with its high residual stresses, elongated grains, and heavily deformed microstructure, is particularly vulnerable to accelerated fatigue, leading to premature failure. In contrast, the HIP sample, characterized by a stress-relieved, recrystallized, and equiaxed grain structure, exhibited enhanced resistance to creep-fatigue damage. The high density of Σ3 twin boundaries further restricted grain boundary sliding, a critical mechanism in high-temperature fatigue, thereby providing additional resistance.

The need for multiple cracks to nucleate (as opposed to one dominant site) is indicative of the material’s improved fatigue resistance; in essence, the material was so resistant to crack initiation that no single flaw was sufficient to cause failure, until several sites ultimately fractured. These cracks grew slowly and only coalesced after a prolonged period of cycling (consistent with the higher fatigue life of HIP samples at room temperature). The fracture surface showed evidence of this delayed crack growth: fatigue striations or crack arrest marks around each initiation site are fine and closely spaced, suggesting a slower propagation rate. When the cracks eventually merged, the final failure occurred by ductile overload, as shown by extensive dimpled rupture in the final fracture region. This large ductile failure zone, combined with the fine fatigue features, is consistent with a high overall damage tolerance and fatigue endurance. In summary, the room-temperature HIP specimen’s fractography demonstrated that crack initiation was difficult and crack propagation was gradual, a direct result of the near absence of internal defects and the beneficial microstructure produced by HIP. This aligned with earlier observations that, although HIP samples had slightly lower absolute fatigue limit at 25 °C than as-built due to microstructural softening, they still exhibited more reliable and gradual failure modes (lower scatter and no catastrophic defect-driven breaks). The multiple initiation sites on a smooth surface underscore that the HIP material’s fatigue failure at ambient conditions was governed by microstructural fatigue mechanisms rather than singular defect-driven initiation, attesting to its enhanced fatigue reliability.

### 3.6. Microstructural evaluation after fatigue

To investigate the microstructural evolution of the specimens following fatigue testing at both ambient temperature and 450 °C, a detailed examination of the fracture edges was conducted. As illustrated in Fig. 13, the fracture zones of the as-built samples revealed distinct microstructural responses under the two testing conditions. Compared with the initial as-built microstructure (Fig. 4e), the overall grain morphology and crystallographic orientation near the fracture region remained relatively unchanged, suggesting that deformation alone did not significantly affect local texture.

Fig. 13, Fig. 13 present the KAM maps for samples fractured at ambient and elevated temperatures, respectively. Compared to the initial as-built sample (Fig. 8b), both fatigue-tested samples exhibited a marked increase in local misorientation, indicating elevated internal strain. In the original condition, stresses were primarily localized near melt pool boundaries due to residual thermal stresses induced during solidification. However, in fatigue-tested specimens, significant misorientation within the grain interiors was observed. This was a consequence of cyclic plastic deformation, which activated dislocation multiplication and accumulation within grains, contributing to increased local misorientation and enhanced stored energy in the microstructure. Interestingly, exposure to elevated temperature (450 °C) did not diminish the microstructural stress effects, contrary to expectations of thermal relaxation. This outcome can be attributed to the prevailing influence of cyclic loading-induced strain hardening and dislocation entanglement, which continuously generate internal stresses at a rate surpassing that of thermally activated recovery. 
At elevated temperatures, the performance trend reversed in comparison with room temperature samples. The as-built microstructure underwent accelerated degradation due to thermally activated processes such as grain coarsening, pore coalescence, and enhanced dislocation mobility. These phenomena, combined with pre-existing residual stresses and microstructural inhomogeneity, contribute to faster crack initiation and propagation. In contrast, the HIP sample, with its homogenized and densified microstructure, exhibited superior thermal stability. Despite increased plastic deformation and dislocation accumulation, the absence of initial porosity and the inherently stress-relieved condition inhibited premature crack nucleation. Furthermore, the more uniform grain structure of HIP samples resisted localized strain accumulation, delaying fatigue damage under high-temperature cyclic loadings. Thus, the enhanced fatigue resistance of HIP samples at elevated temperatures stems from their superior thermal stability, reduced defect population, and more homogeneous microstructural response to mechanical and thermal stimuli.

These findings are particularly relevant to demanding applications such as the energy and nuclear sectors, where components are routinely exposed to sustained cyclic stresses at elevated temperatures. Steam turbine blades, nuclear reactor internal components, impellers, and heat-exchanger tubing require not only high strength but also exceptional thermal stability and resistance to fatigue damage, both at ambient and elevated temperatures (∼ 450 °C). The improved high-temperature fatigue resistance observed in HIP-PBF-LB_SS316L highlights its potential as a safer and more reliable material choice in these environments, supporting extended service lifetimes and reducing the risk of catastrophic failures under critical operating conditions. Beyond defect elimination and microstructural homogenization, the HIP samples (green and red, Fig. 7) show a significantly smaller reduction in fatigue strength with increasing temperature compared to the as-built (blue and black), indicating superior reliability of the HIP for industrial use of PBF-LB produced parts.

## 5. Summary and conclusions

This study comprehensively assessed the impact of Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) on the rotating bending fatigue (RBF) behavior of PBF-LB_SS316L at both ambient (25 °C) and elevated temperatures (450 °C). Through detailed microstructural, mechanical, and fractographic evaluations, the dual effects of HIP were revealed: a slight reduction in fatigue strength at room temperature but a pronounced improvement in fatigue resistance under high-temperature cyclic loading. The observed trends were linked to fundamental microstructural transformations induced by HIP, including recrystallization, porosity elimination, and twin boundary formation, which collectively enhanced thermal stability and fatigue reliability. Some key findings of this study can be listed as below:

  * 1.

Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1150 °C/100 MPa for 4 h produced fully recrystallized, equiaxed grains with Σ3 twin boundary fraction rising from ∼2.4 % to ∼33 %, and nearly eliminated porosity. HIP reduced yield stress and ultimate tensile strength due to the dissolution of cellular substructures and loss of work-hardening features, but it increased ductility significantly (up to ∼80 % elongation).

  * 2.

At an ambient temperature, as-built samples retained finer sub-grain features and higher dislocation densities, providing a higher endurance limit (240 MPa vs. 220 MPa for HIP).

  * 3.

At 450 °C, HIP samples exhibited a higher endurance limit (170 MPa vs. 130 MPa) and enhanced fatigue life retention due to enhanced thermal stability and twin boundary strengthening.

  * 4.

Failures in as-built samples were dominated by multiple defect-driven crack initiation sites, while HIP specimens showed more stable crack growth from a single initiation point, improving fatigue reliability.

  * 5.

HIP microstructures resisted grain coarsening and dislocation accumulation at the elevated temperature, reducing susceptibility to creep-assisted crack growth and grain boundary sliding.
